growth_story.headline: Steady but slow: income per person in the Netherlands has grown about 1.5 percent a year since 1990, through a housing bust, the pandemic and an energy shock.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, growth in income per person in the Netherlands has had no lasting break: it averaged 1.5 percent a year over 1990–2025, one long era. Inside that era came a strong run in the late 1990s, with growth of 4.3 percent in 1999, then a fall of 4.2 percent in 2009 and a second dip in 2012 and 2013, when the IMF describes indebted households saving after a fall in house prices. Growth averaged 0.8 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 1.3 percent over 2016–2025, below the structural-peer median of 1.7. After a drop of 4.4 percent in 2020, income per person bounced back by 5.7 percent in 2021 and 4.0 percent in 2022, then fell 1.6 percent in 2023 as the energy crisis and tighter credit hit. It reached a new peak in 2025, but only just above the level first reached in 2022, and the IMF and OECD describe labour shortages, weak investment, grid congestion and nitrogen limits holding back productivity.

threads.title: Housing bust and household debt
threads.text: After 2008, house prices fell and many households were left with large mortgages. They cut spending and saved, so the economy slipped back into recession in 2012 and 2013. Exports and investment led the recovery that began in 2014.

citations.title: Press Release: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2014 Article IV Consultation with the Netherlands
citations.quote: Exports are rising on expanding global trade; consumption remains sluggish as indebted households continue to save.

citations.title: Kingdom of the Netherlands—Netherlands: 2015 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the Kingdom of the Netherlands—Netherlands (IMF Country Report No. 16/45)
citations.quote: A moderate recovery is underway after a double-dip recession that ended in early 2014.

threads.title: The 2022–23 energy crisis
threads.text: A strong rebound after the pandemic gave way to stagnation when energy prices jumped and financial conditions tightened. Higher prices cut households' buying power, and weaker demand abroad added to the drag. Growth picked up again from 2024.

citations.title: Kingdom of the Netherlands–The Netherlands: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: reflecting the energy shock, tighter financial conditions, and weaker external demand

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Netherlands 2025
citations.quote: Following a strong post-pandemic recovery, GDP stagnated due to the energy crisis, before picking up from the second quarter of 2024

threads.title: Supply limits and weak investment
threads.text: The IMF and OECD describe an economy pressing against its limits: too few workers, a congested electricity grid, nitrogen rules that hold up building, and a shortage of homes. Firms and households save a lot but invest little at home, and productivity has grown slowly.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Netherlands 2025
citations.quote: Persistent supply constraints have been weighing on potential growth, leading to labour shortages, weak investment, and sluggish productivity.

citations.title: Kingdom of The Netherlands—The Netherlands: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/197)
citations.quote: Structural bottlenecks, high savings, and low investment continue to limit the economy's capacity to adapt.

threads.title: High-tech strength, trade exposure
threads.text: The Netherlands is a small, very open trading economy with strong clusters in semiconductors, photonics, fintech and agrifood. That strength also ties growth to foreign suppliers and buyers at a time of rising geopolitical tensions.

citations.title: Kingdom of The Netherlands—The Netherlands: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/197)
citations.quote: Heavy reliance on foreign inputs and demand heightens vulnerability to fragmentation and supply chain disruptions.

since_last_year.text: A new shock arrived in 2026. Energy prices rose with the war in the Middle East, and the IMF expects growth to slow and inflation to pick up again, just as the economy had regained momentum in 2025.

citations.title: Kingdom of The Netherlands—The Netherlands: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/197)
citations.quote: the energy price shock from the war in the Middle East is projected to slow growth to about 1 percent

growth_story.tension: The IMF and OECD describe an economy that weathered crises well and did better than several other euro area economies. Income per person tells a flatter story: it fell 1.6 percent in 2023, when the IMF reports total output still edged up, and in 2025 it stood only just above the level first reached in 2022. The gap comes from a growing population, which the IMF notes has kept adding workers, so total output has grown faster than income per person.
